This view of sin as an involuntary affection of the soul follows logically from another Platonic principle already enunciated by our author (see xxiii., note). This principle is the pre-existence of the soul. The soul, as such, according to Platonic teaching, is wholly good. Evil, therefore, cannot arise from its voluntary preferences, but from its limitations, i.e. from its physical from its relation to the body and from wrong education. In the Book of Wisdom this view is widely diverged from. There the body is not held to be irredeemably evil, but souls and moral environment, are already good and bad on their entrance into this life (viii.

19). In Philo, on the other hand, there is in the main a return to the Platonic and Stoic doctrine. The body is irredeemably evil; it is in fact the tomb of the soul (--); and only the sensuously-inclined souls are incorporated with bodies (see above, xxiii., note). The views adopted by our author on these and kindred points stand in some degree in a closer relation to the Platonic principles than do those of Philo or the author of the Book of Wisdom. Thus he held: (1) That the soul was created originally good. (2) That it was not predetermined either to good or ill by God, but left to mould its own destiny (see xxx.).
